module_title: Secure and Resilient Architectures — Encryption and Key Management
review_basis: Original SAP Module 03 16:9 WebP visuals 01–08 individually inspected and narration follows exact depicted examples, technical labels and caveats.
part_title: Encryption Boundaries, Envelope Encryption and KMS Key Choices

scenes.title: Three encryption questions for every data flow
scenes.visual_overview: Three panels show network transport, encryption at rest, and secure management of credentials and sensitive values.
visual_walkthrough: Follow client to application through TLS
Inspect object, database and volume data keys under AWS KMS
Identify secrets storage, rotation and retrieval controls
scenes.visual_example: A web app uses TLS on the client connection, KMS-integrated encryption for its data storage and a secrets management service for database credentials.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Different data boundaries require different controls; encryption at rest does not replace TLS or secrets management.
scenes.narration: This opening slide asks three security questions about any application data flow. Read the three colored panels from left to right. First, in transit: the user device connects to the application through TLS, with the certificate and TLS version shown in the picture. TLS protects that network connection, but check every additional hop as well, such as between a load balancer and backend. Second, at rest: the middle panel separates the AWS KMS key from a data key used to encrypt stored data. The icons below represent object storage, databases and block volumes. Typically a data key encrypts application data, while a KMS key protects that data key. Third, secrets: the safe and rotation icon represents credentials and other sensitive configuration values. Encryption alone is not a complete credential lifecycle. Prefer controlled access, secure retrieval, rotation where supported and auditing. The bottom question ties the panels together: identify every trust boundary, who owns the encryption keys and how recovery will work. A secure design handles transit, storage and secrets independently.

scenes.title: Envelope encryption: KMS key and data key have different jobs
scenes.visual_overview: The protected KMS key, short-lived plaintext data key and encrypted data are shown in three large visual panels.
visual_walkthrough: KMS key remains controlled by KMS
Data key is used locally only while needed
Ciphertext plus an encrypted copy of the data key can be stored together
scenes.visual_example: A service requests a data key, encrypts a file locally, stores the encrypted file with the encrypted data key, and later obtains an authorized KMS Decrypt operation to recover the plaintext data key.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Envelope encryption avoids sending all large application data to KMS; protect plaintext data keys in memory and authorize decryption carefully.
scenes.narration: This slide explains the two layers in envelope encryption. On the left is the AWS KMS key, illustrated inside a protected vault. It is the long-lived cryptographic key resource that helps protect a data key. The middle panel shows a data key. Application code or an integrated AWS service uses the plaintext data key for data encryption only while necessary, and should minimize its exposure in memory. The right panel is the data itself, encrypted by that data key. Now look at the strip along the bottom. You can store the encrypted data together with an encrypted copy of the data key. To decrypt later, an authorized caller sends the encrypted data key to KMS, obtains the plaintext data key when permitted, and uses it to decrypt the ciphertext. This differs from calling KMS to encrypt every large block of data directly. KMS key policies, grants, key availability and logging are therefore critical even when the encrypted data resides in another service. Remember: the KMS key protects the data key, and the data key encrypts the actual information.

scenes.title: Three levels of KMS key control
scenes.visual_overview: Side-by-side cards distinguish AWS owned, AWS managed and customer managed KMS keys.
visual_walkthrough: AWS owned keys are service-owned and not visible to customers as KMS keys in their account
AWS managed keys appear in an account but have AWS-controlled key policies and lifecycle
Customer managed keys provide customer-controlled policies, grants and supported rotation choices
scenes.visual_example: For an S3 workload requiring specific cross-account decrypt permissions and fine-grained key controls, select a customer managed KMS key rather than relying on an AWS managed key.
scenes.visual_synthesis: The strongest governance decision depends on who needs to control access, audit and cross-account use.
scenes.narration: This slide compares three levels of AWS encryption key management. Start on the left. An AWS owned key belongs to the AWS service and is not exposed as a manageable KMS key in your account. It provides encryption with minimal key administration, but not custom key policies. Move to the middle, an AWS managed key. The key is visible in your account, but AWS controls its policy and lifecycle. These keys simplify integration for supported services, yet do not offer the same customer-directed cross-account access patterns. On the right, a customer managed KMS key gives the organization control over key policy, supported grants, aliases, lifecycle operations and rotation choices. The final green strip emphasizes the architecture decision: if the service must share encrypted resources across accounts or meet special governance rules, a customer managed key often provides the required policy control. That flexibility adds responsibility: permissions, key availability, usage charges, rotation and recovery must be managed. The exam choice is not simply strongest encryption; it is the level of key control the workload actually requires.
